claim: Ubiquilins (Ubqlns) are a family of ubiquitin receptors that promote the delivery of hydrophobic and aggregated ubiquitinated proteins to the proteasome for degradation.
source: Ubiquilins (Ubqlns) are a family of ubiquitin receptors that promote the delivery of hydrophobic and aggregated ubiquitinated proteins to the proteasome for degradation.
evidence: This is a general statement about Ubiquilins' function, supported by established scientific knowledge and citations in the introduction.

claim: When UBQLN1 expression was acutely inhibited, 120 mitochondrial proteins were enriched in the cytoplasm.
source: When UBQLN1 expression was acutely inhibited, 120 mitochondrial proteins were enriched in the cytoplasm, suggesting that the accumulation of mitochondrial client proteins in the absence of UBQLN1 is cytostatic.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from proteomic analysis of BJAB cells with UBQLN1 knockdown.

claim: B cell receptor (BCR) ligation of Ubqln1−/− B cells led to a defect in cell cycle entry.
source: Using a Ubqln1−/− mouse strain, we found that B cell receptor (BCR) ligation of Ubqln1−/− B cells led to a defect in cell cycle entry.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from Ubqln1 knockout mice.

claim: Mitochondrial proteins accumulated in BCR-stimulated Ubqln1−/− cells, leading to protein synthesis inhibition and cell cycle block.
source: As in BJAB cells, mitochondrial proteins accumulated in BCR-stimulated cells, leading to protein synthesis inhibition and cell cycle block.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from BCR-stimulated Ubqln1−/− B cells.

claim: UBQLN1 plays an important role in clearing mislocalized mitochondrial proteins upon cell stimulation.
source: Thus, UBQLN1 plays an important role in clearing mislocalized mitochondrial proteins upon cell stimulation, and its absence leads to suppression of protein synthesis and cell cycle arrest.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: Ubqlns have a ubiquitin-like domain (UBL) that binds to the proteasome.
source: Ubiquilins (Ubqlns) belong to a family of UBL/UBA proteins that link proteasomes with ubiquitinated protein cargo through a ubiquitin-like domain (UBL) that binds to the proteasome (Elsasser et al., 2002; Elsasser et al., 2004; Shi et al., 2016)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Ubqlns have a ubiquitin-binding domain (UBA) that is capable of binding mono- and polyubiquitin chains.
source: and a ubiquitin-binding domain (UBA) that is capable of binding mono- and polyubiquitin chains (Funakoshi et al., 2002; Kleijnen et al., 2000; Ko et al., 2004; Zhang et al., 2008; Zhang et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The UBA domain of Ubqlns shows limited specificity for particular ubiquitin linkages.
source: While the UBA domain of Ubqlns appears to show limited specificity for particular ubiquitin linkages (Zhang et al., 2008)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: In yeast, the Ubqln ortholog DSK2 is required for proteasome-mediated degradation of a subset of polyubiquitinated proteins.
source: In yeast, the Ubqln ortholog DSK2  is required for proteasome-mediated degradation of a subset of polyubiquitinated proteins (Shi et al., 2016; Funakoshi et al., 2002; Verma et al., 2004; Elsasser and Finley, 2005; Lim et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research in yeast.

claim: UBQLN1 binds to a variety of mitochondrial transmembrane proteins and is necessary for the delivery of mislocalized mitochondrial proteins for proteasomal degradation.
source: Recently, Itakura et al. (Itakura et al., 2016) reported that UBQLN1 binds to a variety of mitochondrial transmembrane proteins and is necessary for the delivery of mislocalized mitochondrial proteins for proteasomal degradation.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to recent research by Itakura et al.

claim: After 48 hr of culture with doxycycline, BJABs expressing the UBQLN1 shRNA construct had lost >85% of UBQLN1 protein and roughly 35% of UBQLN2 protein.
source: After 48 hr of culture with doxycycline, BJABs expressing the UBQLN1 shRNA construct had lost >85% of UBQLN1 protein and roughly 35% of UBQLN2 protein (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: BJAB survival and proliferation were profoundly sensitive to the loss of UBQLN1.
source: Unlike other tested cell lines (Itakura et al., 2016; N'Diaye et al., 2009b), BJAB survival and proliferation were profoundly sensitive to the loss of UBQLN1 (Figure 1B–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1B-D and comparison with cited studies.

claim: Loss of proliferation was due to depletion of UBQLN1, since the loss in cell proliferation was strongly correlated with the amount of UBQLN1 depletion for each shRNA tested.
source: Loss of proliferation was due to depletion of UBQLN1, since the loss in cell proliferation was strongly correlated with the amount of UBQLN1 depletion for each shRNA tested (Figure 1—figure supplement 1 )
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing correlation between UBQLN1 depletion and proliferation loss.

claim: The loss of proliferation was rapidly reversed upon removal of doxycycline from the culture.
source: and the loss of proliferation was rapidly reversed upon removal of doxycycline from the culture (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: More than 5100 proteins were quantified in the TMT-MS3 analysis of BJAB cytosol, 1284 of which were significantly altered (p<0.05) between normal and Ubqln1-depleted cells.
source: More than 5100 proteins were quantified, 1284 of which were significantly altered (p<0.05 of a Student's T test) between normal and Ubqln1-depleted cells (Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry data.

claim: DAVID pathway analysis for the cellular compartment of proteins enriched by at least 2-fold upon UBQLN1 depletion (92 proteins) demonstrated a strong mitochondrial protein signature in the cytosol of UBQLN1-depleted cells.
source: DAVID pathway analysis (Huang et al., 2009) for the cellular compartment of proteins enriched by at least 2-fold upon UBQLN1 depletion (92 proteins) demonstrated a strong mitochondrial protein signature in the cytosol of UBQLN1-depleted cells, which was validated by cross-referencing our entire dataset with proteins annotated by Mitocarta 2.0 (Calvo et al., 2016) (Figure 1F and Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by bioinformatics analysis of mass spectrometry data.

claim: There was an enrichment of hydrophobic proteins among those that accumulated in UBQLN1-depleted cytosol, many of which are known to be localized to the mitochondrion in wild-type cells.
source: We found an enrichment of hydrophobic proteins among those that accumulated in UBQLN1-depleted cytosol, many of which are known to be localized to the mitochondrion in wild-type cells (Figure 1G and Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by GRAVY score analysis of mass spectrometry data.

claim: None of the 12 mitochondrially encoded mitochondrial proteins were quantified in the dataset.
source: None of the 12 mitochondrially encoded mitochondrial proteins were quantified in our dataset (Figure 1—source data 1), suggesting that the observed enrichment of mitochondrial proteins in the cytosol was not due to rupture of damaged mitochondria or to opening of the mitochondrial transition pore.
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry data and leads to an inference about the mechanism.

claim: Mislocalized nucleus-encoded mitochondrial proteins make up the dominant fraction of UBQLN1 substrates in BJAB cells.
source: Thus, mislocalized nucleus-encoded mitochondrial proteins make up the dominant fraction of UBQLN1 substrates in this system, consistent with the model presented by Itakura et al. (2016).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data and comparison with cited work.

claim: There was a major increase of unprocessed ATP5G1 in the cytosol, but not mitochondria, of BJABs after induction of UBQLN1 shRNA.
source: There was a major increase of unprocessed ATP5G1 in the cytosol, but not mitochondria, of BJABs after induction of UBQLN1 shRNA (Figure 1H).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: In the cytosol, there was approximately 10- to 20-fold higher levels of ATP5G1 following UBQLN1 depletion.
source: In the cytosol, we found approximately 10- to 20-fold higher levels of ATP5G1 following UBQLN1 depletion (Figure 1I).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification of western blot data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: Ubqln1 knockout mice were generated by deleting exon 2.
source: To understand the significance of UBQLN1 loss in normal B cell physiology, we generated Ubqln1 knockout (-/-) mice by deleting exon 2 (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the description of the knockout strategy shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Loss of Ubqln1 mRNA and protein was confirmed by RT-PCR and western blot.
source: Loss of Ubqln1 mRNA and protein was confirmed by RT-PCR and western blot (Figure 2B–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2B-C.

claim: Ubqln1−/− mice were generally healthy, and no gross anatomical abnormalities were observed.
source: Mice were generally healthy, and we observed no gross anatomical abnormalities.
evidence: This is an observation from the phenotypic characterization of the knockout mice.

claim: Immunophenotyping of Ubqln1−/− mice demonstrated a deficiency of peritoneal B1a cells.
source: However, immunophenotyping of Ubqln1−/− mice demonstrated a deficiency of peritoneal B1a cells (Figure 2D)
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: B1a cells uniquely self-renew in the peritoneum by a pathway dependent on BCR signaling.
source: B1a cells are a subset of B1 cells that express CD5 and, like all B1 cells, they uniquely self-renew in the peritoneum by a pathway dependent on BCR signaling (Lam and Rajewsky, 1999; Hayakawa et al., 1985).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Ubqln1−/− mice had normal numbers of total splenic B-cells.
source: Ubqln1−/− mice had normal numbers of total splenic B-cells (Figure 2E–F)
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figures 2E-F.

claim: Ubqln1−/− mice had normal proportions of transitional B-cell populations.
source: normal proportions of transitional B-cell populations (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Ubqln1−/− mice had normal serum IgM and IgG levels.
source: and normal serum IgM and IgG levels (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: A modest dysregulation of splenic B-cell populations from the marginal zone and follicles was observed in Ubqln1−/− mice.
source: However, we did observe a modest dysregulation of splenic B-cell populations from the marginal zone and follicles (Figure 2G–H).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figures 2G-H.

claim: After 72 hr in culture with anti-IgM, approximately 27% of WT B cells were alive, whereas only ~12% of Ubqln1−/− B cells were viable.
source: After 72 hr in culture with anti-IgM, approximately 27% of WT B cells were alive, whereas only ~12% of Ubqln1−/− B cells were viable (Figure 3A–B).
evidence: This claim is supported by cell viability assay data shown in Figures 3A-B.

claim: Most wild-type cells divided more than once during 72 hr culture with anti-IgM, while the majority of Ubqln1−/− B cells failed to divide more than once.
source: Furthermore, most wild-type cells divided more than once during this period, while the majority of Ubqln1−/− B cells failed to divide more than once (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by CFSE dilution data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: B cells activated via BCR crosslinking undergo a c-MYC-dependent increase in cell size and protein content.
source: Before committing to cell division, B cells activated via BCR crosslinking undergo a c-MYC-dependent increase in cell size and protein content (DeFranco et al., 1985; Iritani and Eisenman, 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The c-MYC-dependent increase in cell size and protein content was markedly defective in Ubqln1−/− cells in response to BCR stimulation.
source: This step was markedly defective in Ubqln1−/− cells in response to BCR stimulation (Figure 3D–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figures 3D-E.

claim: These abnormalities were specific for BCR-initiated proliferation, as no defect was found in Ubqln1−/− B cells at the resting state or in response to LPS.
source: These abnormalities were specific for BCR-initiated proliferation, as we found no defect in Ubqln1−/− B cells at the resting state or in response to LPS in comparison to WT B cells (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of experimental data across different stimulation conditions.

claim: Defective proliferation in response to antigen receptor crosslinking was specific to Ubqln1, as neither Ubqln2- nor Ubqln4-deficient B cells showed any abnormality in response to either anti-IgM or LPS.
source: Defective proliferation in response to antigen receptor crosslinking was specific to Ubqln1, as neither Ubqln2- nor Ubqln4-deficient B cells showed any abnormality in response to either anti-IgM or LPS (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from Ubqln2 and Ubqln4 knockout mice shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: For both WT and Ubqln1−/− mice, there was a significant increase in both total and TNP-specific IgM after TNP-ficoll immunization, but no change in IgG levels.
source: For both WT and Ubqln1−/− mice, we saw a significant increase in both total and TNP-specific IgM, but no change in IgG levels (Figure 3F–G).
evidence: This claim is supported by ELISA data from immunized mice shown in Figures 3F-G.

claim: The viability and cell size defects of Ubqln1−/− B cells were at least partially rescued following the addition of costimulation via either IL-4 or anti-CD40 crosslinking together with anti-IgM.
source: Indeed, the viability and cell size defects of Ubqln1−/− B cells were at least partially rescued following the addition of costimulation via either the cytokine IL-4 or anti-CD40 crosslinking together with anti-IgM (Figure 3H–I).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3H-I.

claim: No Ubqln1-dependent differences were found when isolated B cells were stimulated with recombinant BAFF over a 3-day period.
source: We investigated whether BAFFR signaling could compensate for defective BCR signaling in vivo by stimulating isolated B cells with recombinant BAFF over a 3-day period, and found no Ubqln1-dependent differences (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: 10-plexed TMT analysis on whole-cell lysates of WT and Ubqln1−/− B cells at 24 hr post-BCR stimulation quantified roughly 8000 total proteins, 822 of which were significantly altered between WT and Ubqln1−/−.
source: 10-plexed TMT analysis on whole-cell lysates of WT and Ubqln1−/− B cells at 24 hr post-BCR stimulation quantified roughly 8000 total proteins, 822 of which were significantly altered between WT and Ubqln1−/− (Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry data.

claim: Smaller differences were observed in the proteomes of stimulated whole murine B cells as compared to isolated cytosol from BJABs.
source: Overall, we observed smaller differences in the proteomes of stimulated whole murine B cells as compared to isolated cytosol from BJABs (Figure 4A, Figure 4—source data 1), likely because whole-cell extracts are not able to resolve mislocalized proteins in the cytosol from those present in mitochondria.
evidence: This is a comparison of experimental results with an inference about the reason for the difference.

claim: DAVID pathway analysis of proteins enriched at least 1.25-fold in Ubqln1−/− cells demonstrated increased abundance of ER proteins and mitochondrial membrane proteins in the absence of Ubqln1.
source: a DAVID pathway analysis (Huang et al., 2009) of proteins enriched at least 1.25-fold in Ubqln1−/− cells demonstrated increased abundance of ER proteins and mitochondrial membrane proteins in the absence of Ubqln1 (Table 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by bioinformatics analysis of mass spectrometry data.

claim: In silico analysis demonstrated a similar enrichment of hydrophobic proteins in Ubqln1−/− cells as in UBQLN1-depleted BJAB.
source: Furthermore, in silico analysis demonstrated a similar enrichment of hydrophobic proteins in Ubqln1−/− cells as in UBQLN1-depleted BJAB (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by GRAVY score analysis of mass spectrometry data.

claim: B cell activation via the BCR induced prolonged mitochondrial depolarization.
source: B cell activation via the BCR induced prolonged mitochondrial depolarization (Figure 4C), which was not seen with LPS (Souvannavong et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by JC-1 dye measurements shown in Figure 4C and comparison with cited work.

claim: BCR (IgM) and TLR (LPS) stimulation both induced mitochondrial expansion.
source: BCR (IgM) and TLR (LPS) stimulation both induced mitochondrial expansion (Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 2B)
evidence: This claim is supported by Mitotracker measurements shown in Figure 4D.

claim: BCR (IgM) and TLR (LPS) stimulation both induced mitochondrial superoxide production.
source: and mitochondrial superoxide production (Figure 4E).
evidence: This claim is supported by Mitosox measurements shown in Figure 4E.

claim: No Ubqln1-dependent changes were detected in mitochondrial polarity, expansion, or superoxide production.
source: No Ubqln1-dependent changes in these measurements of mitochondrial health were detected
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental results from mitochondrial assays.

claim: No significant loss in mitochondrial output was observed as measured by ATP production and oxygen consumption rate in Ubqln1−/− cells.
source: nor any significant loss in mitochondrial output as measured by ATP production and oxygen consumption rate (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by ATP assay and Seahorse data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: For both WT and Ubqln1−/− cells, peak Annexin V staining was observed at 8–16 hr post-stimulation with anti-IgM.
source: For both WT and Ubqln1−/− cells, we observed peak Annexin V staining at 8–16 hr post-stimulation
evidence: This claim is supported by Annexin V staining data.

claim: At each time point tested there were fewer Ubqln1−/− apoptotic cells compared to WT.
source: and at each time point tested there were fewer Ubqln1−/− apoptotic cells (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by Annexin V staining data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Ubqln1−/− B cells were significantly less likely to enter the cell cycle after BCR ligation, as measured by DNA content, indicating a block in G0 or G1.
source: Moreover, Ubqln1−/− B cells were significantly less likely to enter the cell cycle, as measured by DNA content after BCR ligation, indicating a block in G0 or G1 (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by cell cycle analysis data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Ubqln1-deficient B cells were less likely than wild-type cells both to enter cell cycle and to apoptose in response to BCR ligation.
source: These data demonstrate that Ubqln1-deficient B cells were less likely than wild-type cells both to enter cell cycle and to apoptose in response to BCR ligation.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the experimental data on apoptosis and cell cycle.

claim: SYK, ERK1/2, AKT, and NFkB activation showed similar kinetics in WT and Ubqln1−/− B cells.
source: SYK, ERK1/2, AKT, and NFkB activation showed similar kinetics in WT and Ubqln1−/− B cells (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data of phosphorylated signaling proteins shown in Figure 5C.

claim: No consistent Ubqln1-dependent expression differences were found in resting cells or in response to either BCR or TLR stimulation by RNAseq.
source: While marked differences were seen in gene expression when comparing resting, TLR4-stimulated, and BCR-stimulated cells, no consistent Ubqln1-dependent expression differences were found in resting cells or in response to either BCR or TLR stimulation (Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Proximal BCR signaling is intact in Ubqln1-deficient B cells.
source: These data demonstrate that proximal BCR signaling is intact in Ubqln1-deficient B cells and that a defect in BCR signaling cannot explain the proliferation and apoptosis defects caused by deletion of Ubqln1.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the signaling and gene expression data.

claim: Of the D-type cyclins, only Ccnd2 is required for murine B1a cell development.
source: Of the D-type cyclins, only Ccnd2 is required for murine B1a cell development (Solvason et al., 2000; Geng et al., 2003; Glassford et al., 2003), implying a specialized role in BCR-induced proliferation.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: mRNA for both Ccnd2 and Myc was induced to comparable levels in Ubqln1−/− and WT cells.
source: mRNA for both Ccnd2 and Myc was induced to comparable levels in Ubqln1−/− and WT cells (Figure 6A–B).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNAseq and QPCR data shown in Figures 6A-B.

claim: c-MYC protein accumulated normally in Ubqln1−/− cells after BCR stimulation.
source: c-MYC protein also accumulated normally (Figure 6C–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figures 6C-D.

claim: CCND2 protein levels did not increase in Ubqln1−/− B cells after BCR signaling.
source: In striking contrast, CCND2 protein levels did not increase in Ubqln1−/− B cells after BCR signaling. (Figure 6C–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figures 6C-D.

claim: CCND3 was also decreased in Ubqln1−/− B cells after BCR stimulation.
source: CCND3, which is also expressed in murine B cells and is required for BJAB proliferation (Schmitz et al., 2012), was also decreased in Ubqln1−/− B cells (Figure 6D).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 6D and citation to previous research.

claim: Ubqln1 is required for CCND2 and CCND3 protein upregulation in response to BCR signaling, even though the mRNA response is Ubqln1-independent.
source: Thus, Ubqln1 is required for CCND2 and CCND3 protein upregulation in response to BCR signaling, even though the mRNA response is Ubqln1-independent.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the mRNA and protein data.

claim: When MG132 was added 4 hr after cell activation, c-MYC protein level was increased for both WT and Ubqln1−/− B cells, but there was no significant effect on CCND2 in either WT or Ubqln1−/− B cells.
source: When MG132 was added 4 hr after cell activation, c-MYC protein level was increased for both WT and Ubqln1−/− B cells, but there was no significant effect on CCND2 in either WT or Ubqln1−/− B cells (Figure 7A–B).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data with proteasome inhibitor shown in Figures 7A-B.

claim: MG132 incubation for 4 or 8 hr at 24 hr post-stimulation dramatically increased c-MYC protein levels in WT cells.
source: MG132 incubation for 4 or 8 hr at this later timepoint dramatically increased c-MYC protein levels in WT cells (Figure 7C–D), indicating that proteasomal degradation is a key contributor to low c-MYC levels at late timepoints.
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data with proteasome inhibitor shown in Figures 7C-D.

claim: Ubqln1−/− c-MYC levels were not significantly increased by MG132 incubation at the late timepoint.
source: Ubqln1−/− c-MYC levels were not significantly increased by MG132 incubation at this late timepoint (Figure 7D)
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data with proteasome inhibitor shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Proteasome inhibition did not increase CCND2 levels to the same extent as those of c-MYC in either WT or Ubqln1−/− B cells.
source: Proteasome inhibition did not increase CCND2 levels to the same extent as those of c-MYC in either WT or Ubqln1−/− B cells, indicating that little CCND2 is degraded during this portion of the cell cycle (Figure 7D).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data with proteasome inhibitor shown in Figure 7D.

claim: MG132 incubation in Ubqln1−/− cells did not rescue CCND2 protein to WT levels.
source: Furthermore, MG132 incubation in Ubqln1−/− cells did not rescue CCND2 protein to WT levels (Figure 7D).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data with proteasome inhibitor shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Increased proteasomal degradation did not account for the lack of CCND2 in Ubqln1−/− B cells after BCR stimulation.
source: Thus, increased proteasomal degradation did not account for the lack of CCND2 in Ubqln1−/− B cells after BCR stimulation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the proteasome inhibitor experiments.

claim: There was no difference in cell viability between WT and Ubqln1−/− at 20 hr after the addition of anti-IgM.
source: Although there was no difference in cell viability between WT and Ubqln1−/− under these conditions (Figure 8A)
evidence: This claim is supported by viability data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: There was no defect in protein synthesis in resting Ubqln1−/− B cells.
source: nor any defect in protein synthesis in resting Ubqln1−/− B cells
evidence: This claim is supported by AHA incorporation data.

claim: There was a marked defect in global protein synthesis after BCR stimulation in the absence of Ubqln1.
source: there was a marked defect in global protein synthesis after BCR stimulation in the absence of Ubqln1 (Figure 8B–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by AHA incorporation data shown in Figures 8B-D.

claim: New protein production was modestly Ubqln1-dependent upon LPS stimulation.
source: New protein production was modestly Ubqln1-dependent upon LPS stimulation (Figure 8E)
evidence: This claim is supported by AHA incorporation data shown in Figure 8E.

claim: Protein synthesis in LPS-stimulated Ubqln1−/− cells was still elevated about fourfold compared to BCR-stimulated cells.
source: but was still elevated about fourfold compared to BCR-stimulated cells, indicating that Ubqln1−/− B cells are intrinsically capable of elevating their protein synthesis rate, and translation is particularly inhibited upon BCR stimulation.
evidence: This is a comparison of experimental results with an inference about the mechanism.

claim: Proteasome inhibition decreased accumulation of AHA-labeled proteins over a 4-hr period after BCR ligation in both WT and Ubqln1−/− cells.
source: Proteasome inhibition actually decreased accumulation of AHA-labeled proteins over a 4-hr period after BCR ligation in both WT and Ubqln1−/− cells (Figure 8F), as has been reported (Ding et al., 2006; Vabulas and Hartl, 2005; Wu et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by AHA incorporation data with proteasome inhibitor shown in Figure 8F and citations to previous research.

claim: MG132 did not diminish the difference in accumulation of AHA-labeled proteins between WT and Ubqln1−/−.
source: MG132 did not diminish the difference in accumulation of AHA-labeled proteins between WT and Ubqln1−/−, indicating that this difference in new protein accumulation was not due to increased proteasomal degradation in the absence of Ubqln1.
evidence: This claim is supported by AHA incorporation data with proteasome inhibitor.

claim: BJABs depleted of UBQLN1 synthesize less new protein.
source: We confirmed the defect in protein synthesis in the absence of UBQLN1 in BJAB cells by performing the same metabolic labeling experiment and found that BJABs depleted of UBQLN1 also synthesize less new protein (Figure 8G).
evidence: This claim is supported by AHA incorporation data in BJAB cells shown in Figure 8G.

claim: The loss of UBQLN1 from the BJAB B-cell lymphoma led to a rapid but reversible loss of proliferative capacity.
source: The loss of UBQLN1 from the BJAB B-cell lymphoma led to a rapid but reversible loss of proliferative capacity
evidence: This is a summary of experimental findings from BJAB cells.

claim: A comprehensive quantitative proteomic analysis revealed that the major effect of UBQLN1 was to suppress the accumulation of hydrophobic mitochondrial proteins in the cytosol.
source: and a comprehensive quantitative proteomic analysis revealed that the major effect of UBQLN1 was to suppress the accumulation of hydrophobic mitochondrial proteins in the cytosol.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the proteomic analysis.

claim: This conclusion is consistent with the work of Itakura et al. who reported an accumulation of the mislocalized mitochondrial protein ATP5G1 upon depletion of all Ubqlns.
source: This conclusion is consistent with the work of Itakura et al. (Itakura et al., 2016), who reported an accumulation of the mislocalized mitochondrial protein ATP5G1 upon depletion of all Ubqlns (UBQLN1, UBQLN2, and UBQLN4).
evidence: This claim compares the current findings with cited previous research.

claim: BJAB cells may be hypersensitive to the loss of UBQLN1 due to high expression levels of mitochondrial proteins.
source: Thus, it is possible that BJABs are hypersensitive to the loss of UBQLN1 due to high expression levels of mitochondrial proteins.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed sensitivity of BJAB cells.

claim: BCR ligation induces much greater and more prolonged mitochondrial depolarization than other mitogenic stimuli, such as TLR4 ligation.
source: A likely explanation for this specificity is that BCR ligation induces much greater and more prolonged mitochondrial depolarization than other mitogenic stimuli, such as TLR4 ligation.
evidence: This is an explanation based on experimental observations of mitochondrial depolarization.

claim: Mitochondrial depolarization attenuates the import of mitochondrial proteins.
source: Since mitochondrial depolarization attenuates the import of mitochondrial proteins (Schleyer et al., 1982)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The increased requirement for Ubqln1 in BCR-stimulated B cells appears to be dependent on the combination of increased mitochondrial protein synthesis and decreased mitochondrial protein import.
source: The increased requirement for Ubqln1 in BCR-stimulated B cells therefore appears to be dependent on the combination of increased mitochondrial protein synthesis and decreased mitochondrial protein import.
evidence: This is a mechanistic conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Stimulation of B cells with IL-4 or CD40 in addition to anti-IgM ameliorates BCR signaling-induced mitochondrial depolarization.
source: Stimulation of B cells with IL-4 (53,64) or CD40 (Eeva et al., 2003) in addition to anti-IgM ameliorates BCR signaling-induced mitochondrial depolarization
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The addition of IL-4 or CD40 co-stimuli to anti-IgM rescued B-cell proliferation in the absence of Ubqln1 because these co-stimuli ameliorate mitochondrial depolarization.
source: which could explain why the addition of these co-stimuli to anti-IgM rescued B-cell proliferation in the absence of Ubqln1.
evidence: This is an inference connecting the rescue of proliferation to amelioration of mitochondrial depolarization.

claim: The mitochondria show no obvious functional defect in the absence of Ubqln1 in BCR-stimulated cells.
source: It is interesting that the mitochondria themselves show no obvious functional defect in the absence of Ubqln1 in BCR-stimulated cells.
evidence: This is an observation from the mitochondrial function assays.

claim: Under BCR stimulation conditions, the import machinery is capable of meeting the demand of increased mitochondrial biogenesis, and nuclear-encoded mitochondrial proteins are made in excess to the mitochondrial requirements.
source: This suggests that under these conditions, the import machinery is capable of meeting the demand of increased mitochondrial biogenesis, and that nuclear-encoded mitochondrial proteins are made in excess to the mitochondrial requirements.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation of normal mitochondrial function.

claim: The toxic event is not intrinsic to mitochondria but related to the cytosolic accumulation of mislocalized mitochondrial proteins.
source: In any case, the finding of normal mitochondrial function in Ubqln1-deficient cells emphasizes that the toxic event is not intrinsic to mitochondria but related to the cytosolic accumulation of mislocalized mitochondrial proteins.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation of normal mitochondrial function despite cellular defects.

claim: The important Ubqln1-dependent step in proliferation in response to BCR signaling was translation of at least some of the induced mRNAs, including Cyclin Ds.
